name: Subperiosteal facelift

card.summary: A midface lift done beneath the periosteum, often endoscopically, that repositions cheek tissue vertically; documented mainly in surgeon series from the 1990s onward.
card.note: Wikipedia notes longer postoperative swelling; nerve anatomy around the cheekbone and temple is a recognized surgical concern.

quick.overview:
A subperiosteal facelift frees the soft tissue of the cheek and midface from the facial bones by working beneath the periosteum, the membrane covering bone. The tissue is then repositioned, mainly in an upward direction, to address flattened cheeks and deep nasolabial folds.

Surgeons in the 1990s described open and endoscopic versions, with the endoscopic approach using small incisions hidden in the hair. Available evidence is surgeon-reported series rather than randomized trials.
quick.mechanism: Dissection lifts soft tissue off bone so the whole mask of the face can be moved as a unit and fixed higher. Endoscopes let surgeons see the deep plane through short incisions.
quick.risks: Wikipedia states the technique causes longer postoperative swelling than some alternatives. Anatomical studies highlight nerves in the cheekbone and temple region, such as the zygomaticotemporal nerve, whose injury can cause numbness or pain. General facelift risks include hematoma, nerve injury and scarring.

lead: A subperiosteal facelift is a surgical technique in which the soft tissues of the face are lifted completely off the underlying bone by dissecting beneath the periosteum, then repositioned. It is used to address deep nasolabial folds and sagging cheeks and is often combined with other techniques.[1]

A 1995 report by endoscopic surgeons describes it as particularly suited to remodeling the central third of the face, and states that the endoscope allows upper-face or total-face rejuvenation without incisional scars, while making deep dissection safer and more accurate.[2] A companion 1995 article describes open and endoscopic approaches and states the endoscopic procedure alone is indicated for mild aging (grade I rhytidosis), and in men with alopecia in whom a coronal incision is a problem, where it may be combined with neck surgery.[3]

Evidence consists of surgeon-reported series and anatomical studies; no randomized comparison with other facelifts was found. In looksmaxxing communities it belongs to hardmaxxing, in discussions of midface and cheek restructuring.

paras: In the subperiosteal approach, soft tissue is released from the bone, including retaining attachments, and repositioned in a vertical direction.[1][2] Wikipedia describes it as used across age groups and as causing longer postoperative swelling.[1]
Related Chinese and French reports from the 1990s and 2000 describe combined or modified subperiosteal facelifts and a so-called mask lift, reflecting its spread internationally.[4][5][6]

Subperiosteal dissection of the face was developed in craniofacial surgery; Wikipedia credits Paul Tessier with using subperiosteal dissection through a coronal incision and with showing in 1979 that undermining the orbital rims allowed better elevation of soft tissue and eyebrows.[1] In the mid-1990s, endoscopic versions were published, aiming to avoid long incisions.[2][3] A 1998 article asked whether the evolution from endoscopic to mini-invasive facelift was a logical progression.[7]

A cadaver study of the zygomaticotemporal nerve notes that its injury causes paresthesia in the area it supplies and that it can be entrapped during procedures including endoscopic subperiosteal facelift.[8] A separate anatomical report studies foramina on the zygomatic bone for their clinical significance.[9]
For facelifts generally, complications include hematoma, facial or sensory nerve injury, skin necrosis, scarring and hair loss at incisions.[1]

Human data are surgeon-reported. The 1995 reports describe indications and technique rather than controlled outcomes.[2][3] A 2006 Brazilian paper summarizes a 5-year experience with the technique.[10] Temporal hollowing augmentation with methyl methacrylate has been described as a related but separate procedure for temple volume.[11] No randomized trials comparing subperiosteal with other facelift techniques were found.

timeline.event: Tessier shows that undermining the orbital rims improves elevation of soft tissue and brows.[1]
French report describes a subperiosteal face lift or mask lift.[6]
Endoscopic and open subperiosteal facelift techniques published.[2][3]
